screens.title: The Pillars of Observability
screens.narratorSegment: In modern distributed systems, knowing that a service is running is not enough. Observability is the ability to infer the internal state of a system from its external outputs — the telemetry your services emit. This chapter focuses on the three complementary pillars of observability: metrics, logs, and traces. Metrics give you fast, aggregated signals about system health and trends. Logs provide detailed, timestamped narratives of individual events. Traces reveal how a single request moves across services and which operations consume time. You will learn what each pillar is best at, how they complement one another, and the practical trade‑offs when instrumenting a production system. We will also walk through common pitfalls — like treating observability as an afterthought — and a concrete activity that applies all three pillars to an Orders A P I endpoint. By the end, you should be able to choose the right pillar for a given debugging question and design instrumentation that helps your team diagnose incidents quickly while protecting sensitive data. To begin, notice how the three topic cards below map to real diagnostic questions you will face in system design and operations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define each observability pillar, choose which pillar to use for specific investigation questions, and design basic instrumentation for a microservice endpoint. First, you will learn to distinguish metrics, logs, and traces by their format, typical use cases, and limits. Second, you will understand why combining all three provides the full picture — metrics for rapid detection, logs for event context, and traces for request‑level causality. Third, you'll practice mapping telemetry to a concrete A P I endpoint so you can specify which metrics to collect, which structured logs to emit, and how to model spans in a trace. Finally, you'll recognize key anti‑patterns and privacy concerns, such as incomplete coverage and sensitive data in logs, and be prepared to recommend sanitization and retention choices. Each objective ties directly to a verified competency milestone so you can track progress in system design interviews and on‑call readiness.

screens.title: Metrics: Aggregated time‑series signals
screens.narratorSegment: Metrics are numerical measurements sampled or aggregated over time to represent a system's health or performance. They are typically stored as time‑series and optimized for quick queries and dashboards. Common examples include C P U utilization, requests per second, error rates, queue lengths, and database connection pool usage. Metrics are powerful because they are lightweight and can be retained at high resolution for trend analysis and alerting. For example, when your dashboard shows a sudden spike in latency for the authentication service, that metric points to an anomaly you must investigate. However, metrics alone rarely tell you which specific request or user experienced the problem or the textual error that occurred. A common misconception is to assume metrics give full context; they do not. Metrics answer the question "what is happening at scale" but not "why a particular operation failed." In practice you should design metrics with clear names and labels, ensure low cardinality where appropriate, and capture both counts and latency distributions so you can detect both volume and performance regressions. Example: track requests per second as a counter and latency as a histogram so you can see both traffic bursts and tail latency. Takeaway: metrics are your fast alarm system; they tell you where to look next.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Metrics
Definition
Metrics are time‑series numbers for monitoring and alerting

They show aggregated trends such as CPU, RPS, error rate, and queue length. Metrics are efficient for dashboards and real‑time alerts.

  • Strength: Lightweight, fast queries and clear trends.
  • Limit: Lacks per‑request textual context to explain failures.
Concrete Example
A sudden increase in request latency metric for the auth service triggers an alert so engineers begin deeper investigation using logs and traces.
Visualization
Time-series chart (example):
Timestamp        requests_per_second  p95_latency_ms
2023-01-01T12:00   120                 120
2023-01-01T12:01   125                 122
2023-01-01T12:02   400                 500  <-- sudden spike
2023-01-01T12:03   130                 118
Common Mistake
Treating a single metric spike as full diagnosis without correlating logs and traces.
Key Takeaway
Design metrics for low cardinality and capture both counts and latency distributions.

screens.title: Logs: Detailed event records
screens.narratorSegment: Logs are timestamped records of discrete events, often text or structured JSON, that describe what happened inside a component. Unlike aggregated metrics, logs contain the narrative and context necessary to understand why an operation failed or what data a process handled. For example, an authentication service might emit an INFO log when a user attempts login and an ERROR log with a message and stack trace when authentication fails. Structured logging—emitting key fields such as request_id, user_id, and status—makes it feasible to search and filter logs across many services. Centralized log collection prevents the Sisyphean work of scanning local files on dozens of instances and enables correlation with metrics and traces. A common misconception is that more logs are always better. In reality, unbounded verbose logs create storage and noise problems and can leak sensitive information. You should plan what to log, include identifiers for correlation, and apply sanitization for PII. Example: emit structured log entries with request_id and sanitized user metadata so you can find the exact sequence of events for one failed purchase without exposing full credit card data. Takeaway: logs give you the “why” behind metric alerts when you need detailed context.

keyIdea.title: Logs summary
keyIdea.text: Logs provide detailed context for events and errors; structured, centralized logs enable efficient debugging and correlation.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Logs
What logs provide
Detailed, timestamped records for specific events and errors

Logs show the narrative: who did what, what parameters were used, and what error messages occurred. Structured logs with named fields make queries practical across services.

  • Strength: high fidelity context for individual failures and audits.
  • Limit: high volume and difficulty correlating without IDs and centralization.
Concrete Example
Log entry: { "time": "...", "level": "ERROR", "request_id": "abc123", "message": "Payment failed", "payment_gateway_response": "invalid_card" }. This points to the exact failure for one order.
Practice tips
Emit request identifiers, choose structured fields, centralize collection, and sanitize PII. Balance verbosity with storage cost and searchability.
Pitfall
Unrestricted verbose logs produce noise and potential exposure of sensitive data.
Key Takeaway
Use structured, centralized logs with identifiers for efficient debugging while protecting privacy.

screens.title: Traces and Spans: Follow one request end‑to‑end
screens.narratorSegment: A trace represents the end‑to‑end journey of a single request as it traverses services, and it is composed of spans—each span representing one unit of work with a start time, end time, and metadata. Traces are especially valuable in microservices architectures because they show parent‑child relationships and reveal where latency accumulates. For example, if a page load is slow, a trace can show that 80% of the latency occurred in a downstream database query rather than the frontend or an intermediary A P I. Implementing tracing requires consistent context propagation so that the same trace identifier travels across service boundaries and links spans together. A common misconception is that traces replace logs; they do not. Traces tell you how time flows across services for a single request, while logs give the detailed error messages and context for events within those spans. Concrete example: a root span for /api/orders/create might have child spans for payment gateway call and inventory update. By inspecting the durations of child spans you can pinpoint bottlenecks and prioritize optimizations. Takeaway: traces answer the question of where time is spent during an individual request and expose inter‑service dependencies.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Traces & Spans
Definition
A trace is the end‑to‑end story of a single request composed of spans

Each span records an operation, its duration, and metadata. Parent‑child relationships reveal the call graph and where time was spent.

Concrete Example
Root span: /api/orders/create → Child: payment call (120ms) → Child: inventory update (40ms). The payment span is the dominant latency source.
Practice
Ensure consistent trace ID propagation. Traces complement logs and metrics — they do not replace them. Use traces when intermittent, per‑request latency matters or when you need to map dependencies between services.
Misconception
Assuming traces provide full textual error context; traces give timing and structure, logs supply the textual details.
Key Takeaway
Use traces to locate bottlenecks and map service dependencies for single requests.

screens.title: How to combine metrics, logs, and traces
screens.narratorSegment: A pragmatic incident workflow combines the strengths of metrics, logs, and traces in a few deliberate steps. Start with metrics to detect anomalies: metrics are lightweight and tell you that something changed, such as a latency spike or rising error rates. Next, use logs to surface the textual details of failures — error messages, stack traces, and structured fields like request_id that provide context. If the issue is about where time is spent across services or intermittent slow requests, inspect traces to follow the exact path of affected requests and find the slow spans. For instance, imagine an alert for increased order creation latency. Metrics point you to the affected service and time window. You then filter logs by request_id or timestamp to find errors or unusual inputs that coincide with the spike. If logs alone don't explain a timing problem, examine traces for representative slow requests: the trace will show whether the delay is in the payment gateway call, inventory update, or internal processing. A typical misconception is to look at one pillar in isolation; instead, correlate evidence across pillars to build a complete diagnosis. Closing question: when you see a metric spike with no errors in logs, what trace pattern would you expect to check next? That question guides your next diagnostic step.

keyIdea.title: Diagnostic flow
keyIdea.text: Detect with metrics → investigate with logs → verify and localize with traces to form a complete incident story.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Diagnostic Workflow
Stepwise process
1
Detect with metrics
Use time window and service filter to find anomalies and affected components.
2
Investigate with logs
Search structured logs for request_id, error messages, or unusual state during the window.
3
Localize with traces
Examine spans to see where time is spent and which downstream call is the bottleneck.
Concrete scenario
Alert: order creation latency spike. Metrics show spike at 12:02. Logs filtered by timestamp reveal several ERROR entries with the same request_id indicating payment failures. Traces of slow requests show that the payment span took 800ms while other spans remained short. Root cause: intermittent latency in payment gateway. Fix: add retry/backoff and monitor payment latency metric.
Misconception
Assuming logs alone will reveal distributed timing bottlenecks without trace context.
Key Takeaway
Use the pillars in sequence to detect, investigate, and localize incidents efficiently.

screens.title: Design choices for observability
screens.narratorSegment: Designing observability means making deliberate choices about what to instrument, how to collect telemetry, and how to protect sensitive information. Instrumentation decisions include selecting which metrics to emit, which events to log, and which operations to trace. Centralized collection — a metrics backend, a log aggregator, and a tracing system — makes it possible to correlate data across services. An important safety consideration is that logs and traces can contain sensitive information. Plan sanitization and access controls up front: remove or mask PII and limit who can view raw telemetry. Another architectural challenge is ensuring trace context is propagated consistently so spans link across service boundaries; this often requires library support or middleware. A common misconception is that observability can be bolted on later; in practice, retrofitting consistent tracing and structured logs across many services is costly and error prone. Example: adding trace propagation libraries to each service at design time ensures traces are complete from day one. Takeaway: treat observability as a first‑class concern in system design; plan instrumentation, collection, and privacy together. Design choices for observability means plan instrumentation and collection early; ensure trace propagation and apply sanitization and access control to telemetry.. In practical terms, instrumentation, central collection, and privacy considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Design Choices
Instrumentation
Decide which metrics, logs, and spans are necessary for key user journeys. Instrument the happy path and likely failure modes, and include identifiers for correlation.
Trace propagation
Ensure trace IDs are passed across service calls so spans join into a single trace.
Collection & Privacy
Centralize metrics, logs, and traces for correlation. Apply sanitization rules to logs and control access to raw telemetry to avoid exposing PII or internal secrets.
Trade-offs
Higher fidelity tracing increases overhead; balance detail against cost and performance impact.
Key Takeaway
Design observability early, propagate context, and protect sensitive telemetry with sanitization and access control.

screens.title: Strengths and trade‑offs of each pillar
screens.narratorSegment: Each observability pillar has clear strengths and trade‑offs that guide when to use it. Use metrics when you need real‑time trend detection and lightweight alerts: metrics answer questions like "how many requests per second" or "is error rate increasing?" Use logs when you need textual detail, for auditing, or to inspect the exact inputs and error messages for a particular event. Use traces when you need to understand the end‑to‑end path and timing for individual requests across services. A common interview trap is to blur these roles and try to force one pillar to do another's job: metrics are poor at explaining individual errors, logs are hard to use for timing across services, and traces are not a replacement for detailed error messages. Consider this example: if overall latency metrics remain normal but some users complain of slow responses, traces allow you to inspect specific slow requests and see which span is responsible. Conversely, if error rates suddenly climb, start with metrics and then filter structured logs by the timestamps and request identifiers that metrics highlighted. The practical takeaway is to view the pillars as complementary tools in a diagnostics toolbox, each applied to the question it answers best.

keyIdea.text: Metrics for trends, logs for context, traces for per‑request timing. Avoid expecting one pillar to do everything.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Pillar Comparison
Metrics
Best for trends and alerts. Lightweight, fast queries, limited per‑request context.
Logs
Best for textual context, error messages, and audits. Can be high volume if unchecked.
Traces
Best for per‑request timing and dependency mapping. Requires context propagation.
Decision guide
If you need fast detection, use metrics. If you need the error text or parameters, use logs. If you need to see where time is spent end‑to‑end, use traces. Combine them when resolving production incidents.

screens.title: Instrumenting /api/orders/create — Metrics
screens.narratorSegment: When instrumenting the /api/orders/create endpoint, choose metrics that reveal both volume and performance. Three useful metrics are: a counter for total order creation attempts and successes to track throughput and success rate; a latency distribution (histogram) for the endpoint so you can observe p50, p95, and p99 response times; and a gauge showing the current size of any processing queue or pending orders to detect backpressure. Counters let you detect spikes in traffic or errors, histograms show tail latency and whether rare slow requests exist, and gauges surface resource pressure. A misconception is to track only average latency; averages hide tail behavior that impacts user experience. Example: increment the orders_created counter on success and orders_failed on error; record request latency into the histogram to identify whether p99 latency is rising. Design metrics with labels such as service_instance or region only where cardinality stays manageable, otherwise high-cardinality labels can explode storage and make queries slow. Takeaway: choose metrics that together show throughput, latency distribution, and resource pressure for robust alerting and capacity planning. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.1 › Activity — Metrics
Suggested metrics for /api/orders/create
  • orders_created_total — Counter for successful order creations.
  • orders_failed_total — Counter for failed attempts to create orders.
  • orders_create_latency_ms — Histogram for endpoint latency (p50/p95/p99).
  • pending_orders_queue_size — Gauge for in‑flight or queued order processing.
Key Takeaway
Combine counters, histograms, and gauges so you can monitor throughput, detect failures, and observe tail latency and resource pressure.
Implementation notes
Increment counters at logical success/failure points. Record latency surrounding the request handler. Avoid high‑cardinality labels unless necessary.
Concrete Example

screens.title: Common pitfalls and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: There are several common pitfalls when teams implement observability. Treating instrumentation as an afterthought is costly because retrofitting consistent tracing and structured logs across many services takes time and risks gaps. Instrumenting only a subset of services or only one pillar produces blind spots: you might see a metric spike but have no logs to explain the error or incomplete traces that stop at service boundaries. Another serious concern is exposing sensitive information in logs or traces. Telemetry often carries identifiers and payloads; decide up front what to sanitize and who may view raw data. Implement retention policies to balance debugging needs with privacy and storage cost. A misconception is that more telemetry is always better; unbounded logging and high‑cardinality metrics increase cost and reduce signal‑to‑noise. Example anti‑pattern: adding verbose debug logs in production without sanitization, which creates storage bloat and potential PII exposure. Takeaway: design for observability early, instrument consistently across services, and enforce sanitization and access control so telemetry helps without harming privacy or becoming unmanageable. Common pitfalls and safety notes means avoid partial instrumentation and unfiltered telemetry. plan instrumentation, sanitization, and retention up front.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
In modern distributed systems, knowing that a service is running is not enough. Observability is the ability to infer the internal state of a system from its external outputs — the telemetry your services emit. This chapter focuses on the three complementary pillars of observability: metrics, logs, and traces. Metrics give you fast, aggregated signals about system health and trends. Logs provide detailed, timestamped narratives of individual events. Traces reveal how a single request moves across services and which operations consume time. You will learn what each pillar is best at, how they complement one another, and the practical trade‑offs when instrumenting a production system. We will also walk through common pitfalls — like treating observability as an afterthought — and a concrete activity that applies all three pillars to an Orders A P I endpoint. By the end, you should be able to choose the right pillar for a given debugging question and design instrumentation that helps your team diagnose incidents quickly while protecting sensitive data. To begin, notice how the three topic cards below map to real diagnostic questions you will face in system design and operations.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define each observability pillar, choose which pillar to use for specific investigation questions, and design basic instrumentation for a microservice endpoint. First, you will learn to distinguish metrics, logs, and traces by their format, typical use cases, and limits. Second, you will understand why combining all three provides the full picture — metrics for rapid detection, logs for event context, and traces for request‑level causality. Third, you'll practice mapping telemetry to a concrete A P I endpoint so you can specify which metrics to collect, which structured logs to emit, and how to model spans in a trace. Finally, you'll recognize key anti‑patterns and privacy concerns, such as incomplete coverage and sensitive data in logs, and be prepared to recommend sanitization and retention choices. Each objective ties directly to a verified competency milestone so you can track progress in system design interviews and on‑call readiness.

In addition to conceptual understanding, this chapter asks you to practice three concrete skills that often appear in system design interviews and on‑call exercises. First, pick the right pillar to answer a debugging question: given a metric spike, choose whether to look next at logs to find error details or traces to see slow request paths. Second, design instrumentation for an A P I by naming at least three metrics, three structured logs, and the span hierarchy for a trace. That skill shows you can think end‑to‑end about observability. Third, identify privacy and operational constraints: decide what to sanitize in logs and set retention policies so telemetry supports debugging without exposing sensitive data. Practicing these tasks will prepare you to both design systems and communicate an observability plan under time pressure. These are the applied milestones you will revisit in the hands‑on activity and the assessment examples later in the chapter.

Metrics are numerical measurements sampled or aggregated over time to represent a system's health or performance. They are typically stored as time‑series and optimized for quick queries and dashboards. Common examples include C P U utilization, requests per second, error rates, queue lengths, and database connection pool usage. Metrics are powerful because they are lightweight and can be retained at high resolution for trend analysis and alerting. For example, when your dashboard shows a sudden spike in latency for the authentication service, that metric points to an anomaly you must investigate. However, metrics alone rarely tell you which specific request or user experienced the problem or the textual error that occurred. A common misconception is to assume metrics give full context; they do not. Metrics answer the question "what is happening at scale" but not "why a particular operation failed." In practice you should design metrics with clear names and labels, ensure low cardinality where appropriate, and capture both counts and latency distributions so you can detect both volume and performance regressions. Example: track requests per second as a counter and latency as a histogram so you can see both traffic bursts and tail latency. Takeaway: metrics are your fast alarm system; they tell you where to look next.

Logs are timestamped records of discrete events, often text or structured JSON, that describe what happened inside a component. Unlike aggregated metrics, logs contain the narrative and context necessary to understand why an operation failed or what data a process handled. For example, an authentication service might emit an INFO log when a user attempts login and an ERROR log with a message and stack trace when authentication fails. Structured logging—emitting key fields such as request_id, user_id, and status—makes it feasible to search and filter logs across many services. Centralized log collection prevents the Sisyphean work of scanning local files on dozens of instances and enables correlation with metrics and traces. A common misconception is that more logs are always better. In reality, unbounded verbose logs create storage and noise problems and can leak sensitive information. You should plan what to log, include identifiers for correlation, and apply sanitization for PII. Example: emit structured log entries with request_id and sanitized user metadata so you can find the exact sequence of events for one failed purchase without exposing full credit card data. Takeaway: logs give you the “why” behind metric alerts when you need detailed context.

A trace represents the end‑to‑end journey of a single request as it traverses services, and it is composed of spans—each span representing one unit of work with a start time, end time, and metadata. Traces are especially valuable in microservices architectures because they show parent‑child relationships and reveal where latency accumulates. For example, if a page load is slow, a trace can show that 80% of the latency occurred in a downstream database query rather than the frontend or an intermediary A P I. Implementing tracing requires consistent context propagation so that the same trace identifier travels across service boundaries and links spans together. A common misconception is that traces replace logs; they do not. Traces tell you how time flows across services for a single request, while logs give the detailed error messages and context for events within those spans. Concrete example: a root span for /api/orders/create might have child spans for payment gateway call and inventory update. By inspecting the durations of child spans you can pinpoint bottlenecks and prioritize optimizations. Takeaway: traces answer the question of where time is spent during an individual request and expose inter‑service dependencies.

A pragmatic incident workflow combines the strengths of metrics, logs, and traces in a few deliberate steps. Start with metrics to detect anomalies: metrics are lightweight and tell you that something changed, such as a latency spike or rising error rates. Next, use logs to surface the textual details of failures — error messages, stack traces, and structured fields like request_id that provide context. If the issue is about where time is spent across services or intermittent slow requests, inspect traces to follow the exact path of affected requests and find the slow spans. For instance, imagine an alert for increased order creation latency. Metrics point you to the affected service and time window. You then filter logs by request_id or timestamp to find errors or unusual inputs that coincide with the spike. If logs alone don't explain a timing problem, examine traces for representative slow requests: the trace will show whether the delay is in the payment gateway call, inventory update, or internal processing. A typical misconception is to look at one pillar in isolation; instead, correlate evidence across pillars to build a complete diagnosis. Closing question: when you see a metric spike with no errors in logs, what trace pattern would you expect to check next? That question guides your next diagnostic step.

Designing observability means making deliberate choices about what to instrument, how to collect telemetry, and how to protect sensitive information. Instrumentation decisions include selecting which metrics to emit, which events to log, and which operations to trace. Centralized collection — a metrics backend, a log aggregator, and a tracing system — makes it possible to correlate data across services. An important safety consideration is that logs and traces can contain sensitive information. Plan sanitization and access controls up front: remove or mask PII and limit who can view raw telemetry. Another architectural challenge is ensuring trace context is propagated consistently so spans link across service boundaries; this often requires library support or middleware. A common misconception is that observability can be bolted on later; in practice, retrofitting consistent tracing and structured logs across many services is costly and error prone. Example: adding trace propagation libraries to each service at design time ensures traces are complete from day one. Takeaway: treat observability as a first‑class concern in system design; plan instrumentation, collection, and privacy together. Use metrics when you need real‑time trend detection and lightweight alerts: metrics answer questions like "how many requests per second" or "is error rate increasing?" Use logs when you need textual detail, for auditing, or to inspect the exact inputs and error messages for a particular event. Use traces when you need to understand the end‑to‑end path and timing for individual requests across services.
